title: Macroeconomic objectives II: Economic growth, sustainable level of debt

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes economic growth?
hints: Recall the difference between nominal and real measures of output.
For each option, ask whether it describes a change in what is produced, a change in prices, or a change in inputs.
questions.targets: Real vs nominal measure of growth

options.text: An increase in nominal GDP over a period of time
options.misconception: Nominal GDP can rise only because prices rise, with no extra output produced.

options.text: An increase in real GDP over a period of time
An increase in the average price level over a period of time
options.misconception: This describes inflation, not a rise in the quantity of output.

options.text: An increase in the number of people in the labour force
options.misconception: More workers may help output grow, but it is a cause of growth, not growth itself.

questions.prompt: Veld's real GDP grew by 2% last year. Why would an economist prefer real GDP per capita to real GDP when judging whether average living standards in Veld improved?
hints: Compare what the words 'per capita' add to the real GDP figure.
Ask what could happen to output per person if output rises but something else rises faster.
questions.targets: Why per capita adjustment matters for living standards

options.text: It takes account of changes in the size of the population
It removes the effect of inflation, which real GDP does not
options.misconception: Real GDP is already adjusted for inflation; the per capita step adjusts for something else.

options.text: It includes the value of non-market activities such as unpaid care work
options.misconception: Per capita figures still leave out non-market output, just like total real GDP.

options.text: It shows how income is shared between rich and poor households
options.misconception: An average per person says nothing about how income is distributed.

questions.prompt: Define the term economic growth.
hints: Your definition should refer to a specific measure of output.
Say what happens to that measure and over what kind of period.
questions.targets: Precise definition using real output
marking_points: An increase in real GDP / real output of goods and services [1]
Over a period of time (e.g. from one year to the next) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer states an increase in real GDP (real output) and refers to a time period; 'GDP' alone without 'real' earns only 1.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of natural capital in the country of Kuva?
hints: Use the four types of capital: physical, human, natural and institutional.
Decide which option is provided by nature rather than produced or learned by people.
questions.targets: Classifying types of capital

options.text: A newly built highway linking Kuva's two largest cities
options.misconception: A highway is man-made, so it is physical capital.

options.text: The fish stocks in Kuva's coastal waters
A training programme that improves the skills of Kuva's nurses
options.misconception: Skills and training are part of human capital.

options.text: The money that Kuvan households hold in savings accounts
options.misconception: Savings are financial assets, not a factor of production provided by nature.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between physical capital and human capital.
hints: Think about what each type of capital consists of.
For each one, give what it is and the kind of investment that creates it, with a short example.
questions.targets: Physical vs human capital
marking_points: Physical capital is man-made goods used to produce other goods, such as machines, equipment or roads [1]
Human capital is the skills, knowledge and health of workers, built through spending on education, training and health care [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives a clear description of each type, ideally with an example; one mark for each side of the distinction.

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, what was the rate of economic growth in Veld between 2024 and 2025?
hints: Use the percentage change formula with real GDP.
Find the change between the two years, divide by the earlier year's value and multiply by 100.
questions.targets: Percentage change with the correct base year

options.misconception: This is the absolute increase in zed billion, not a percentage change.
This divides the increase by the 2025 value instead of the starting value.
This is the 2025 figure as a percentage of the 2024 figure, not the rate of change.

questions.prompt: Using Table 2, calculate (i) the rate of economic growth in Veld between 2024 and 2025 and (ii) real GDP per capita in each year. Show your working.
hints: Use the percentage change formula for (i) and divide output by population for (ii).
Keep the units consistent: both real GDP and population are in millions, so the per capita answer is in zed per person.
questions.targets: Growth rate vs per capita change

table.caption: Table 2: Real GDP and population of Veld

marking_points: Real GDP per capita = 500 / 10 = 50 zed in 2024 and 530 / 10.6 = 50 zed in 2025 [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer shows the working and reaches 6% growth and real GDP per capita of 50 zed in both years; a strong student notes per capita output did not change despite growth.

questions.prompt: Table 3 shows output and hours worked in Kuva. Which statement about labour productivity is correct?
hints: Productivity is measured as output per hour of work.
Work out output divided by hours for each year separately, then compare.
questions.targets: Output vs output per hour

table.caption: Table 3: Output and hours worked in Kuva

options.text: Productivity rose, because total output increased
options.misconception: A rise in total output can come from more hours worked, not from more output per hour.

options.text: Productivity fell from 3.0 to 2.8 units per hour
Productivity rose from 3.0 to 3.5 units per hour
options.misconception: This divides Year 2 output by Year 1 hours, mixing the two years.

options.text: Productivity was unchanged, because output and hours both rose
options.misconception: Both rose, but by different percentages, so output per hour changed.

questions.prompt: Using Table 4, calculate labour productivity in Veld in each year and the percentage change in productivity between the two years.
hints: Productivity is output divided by hours worked.
Find the value for each year first, then apply the percentage change formula using the first year as the base.
questions.targets: Productivity level and its percentage change

table.caption: Table 4: Real output and hours worked in Veld

marking_points: Year 1: 2,000 / 400 = 5 zed of output per hour; Year 2: 2,160 / 400 = 5.4 zed per hour [1]
Percentage change = (5.4 − 5) / 5 × 100 [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives both productivity figures (5 and 5.4 zed per hour) and an 8% increase with working shown.

questions.prompt: The government of Kuva greatly expands vocational training for young workers. On a production possibilities curve (PPC) diagram, which change best shows the long-term effect on economic growth?
hints: Ask whether training changes how much the economy is able to produce at full employment.
A change in the economy's productive capacity is shown differently from a change in how fully resources are used.
questions.targets: Actual vs potential growth on a PPC

options.text: A movement from a point inside the PPC to a point on the PPC
options.misconception: This shows the use of previously unemployed resources, which is short-term growth.

options.text: A movement along the PPC towards more capital goods
options.misconception: This shows a change in the output mix, not an increase in what the economy can produce.

options.text: A movement from a point on the PPC to a point inside it
options.misconception: This shows a loss of output, such as during a recession.

options.text: An outward shift of the whole PPC

questions.prompt: Veld's economy is in a recession with high unemployment. Which of the following is most likely to cause short-term growth without increasing potential output?
hints: Short-term growth is linked to aggregate demand; long-term growth is linked to productive capacity.
For each option, decide whether it changes the economy's resources or only the level of spending.
questions.targets: Demand-side (actual) vs supply-side (potential) causes of growth

options.text: Discovery of large new reserves of natural gas
options.misconception: New resources raise the economy's productive capacity, which is long-term growth.

options.text: A rise in the number of university graduates
options.misconception: More graduates improve human capital and raise potential output.

options.text: A rise in consumer confidence that increases household spending
Adoption of new technology that raises output per worker
options.misconception: Better technology raises productivity and shifts potential output outwards.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between short-term economic growth and long-term economic growth. You may refer to a PPC or an AD/AS diagram in words.
hints: Use the ideas of actual output and potential output.
For each type, say what causes it and how it would appear on a PPC or AD/AS diagram.
questions.targets: Actual vs potential growth, with causes and diagrams
marking_points: Short-term growth is an increase in actual real output, often by using unemployed resources [1]
It is shown as a movement from inside the PPC towards the curve, or a rightward AD shift with a recessionary gap [1]
Long-term growth is an increase in potential output / productive capacity, from more or better resources [1]
It is shown as an outward shift of the PPC or a rightward shift of LRAS [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer explains both types with a cause and correctly describes how each appears on a diagram.

questions.prompt: Explain how increased government spending on education and health care in Kuva could lead to long-term economic growth. Refer to a diagram in your answer.
hints: Think about which type of capital this spending builds and how it affects workers.
Link the effect on workers to output per hour, then to productive capacity, and state the shift on a PPC or LRAS diagram.
questions.targets: Human capital to potential output chain
marking_points: Spending on education and health increases human capital (skills, knowledge, health of workers) [1]
Workers become more productive, producing more output per hour [1]
This increases the economy's productive capacity / potential output [1]
Shown as an outward shift of the PPC or a rightward shift of the LRAS curve [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer builds the chain from spending to human capital to productivity to potential output and names the correct diagram shift.

questions.prompt: Real GDP in Veld has grown by 4% a year for a decade. Explain two reasons why this growth may not have improved living standards for all of Veld's people.
hints: Consider how the extra output is shared and what real GDP does not capture.
For each reason, state it and then explain how it stops some people's living standards rising.
questions.targets: Limits of growth as a measure of well-being
marking_points: Reason 1 identified, e.g. benefits of growth are unequally distributed [1]
Explained, e.g. most extra income goes to high-income groups so low-income households see little change [1]
Reason 2 identified, e.g. population grows as fast as output / environmental damage / longer working hours [1]
Explained, e.g. real GDP per capita barely rises, or pollution harms health, lowering quality of life [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives two distinct reasons, each with a clear link to why some people's living standards do not improve.

questions.prompt: Veld's government debt was zed 100 billion at the start of Year 1. Using Table 5, what was the government debt at the end of Year 3?
hints: Government debt is built up from past budget balances.
Start with the opening debt, add each deficit and subtract each surplus.
questions.targets: Deficit/surplus as flows, debt as a stock

table.caption: Table 5: Budget balance of the government of Veld

options.text: zed 130 billion
options.misconception: This adds the surplus as if it were another deficit.

options.text: zed 120 billion
zed 20 billion
options.misconception: This is only the net change in debt; the starting debt must be included.

options.text: zed 95 billion
options.misconception: This applies only the final year's surplus and ignores the earlier deficits.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a budget deficit and government debt.
hints: One of these is measured over a period of time and the other at a point in time.
State what each one is and how the two are connected.
questions.targets: Flow vs stock
marking_points: A budget deficit occurs when government expenditure exceeds tax revenue in a given period (e.g. one year) [1]
Government debt is the total amount owed, the accumulation of past deficits minus surpluses [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer defines the deficit as a yearly shortfall and debt as the accumulated total owed.

questions.prompt: Using Table 6, what was Kuva's debt-to-GDP ratio in 2025?
hints: Use the debt-to-GDP ratio formula.
Divide government debt by GDP and multiply by 100.
questions.targets: Correct numerator and denominator

options.misconception: This divides GDP by debt, turning the ratio upside down.
This is the gap between GDP and debt as a share of GDP, not debt as a share of GDP.
This treats the debt figure itself as a percentage.

questions.prompt: Using Table 7, calculate Veld's debt-to-GDP ratio in 2024 and 2025. State what the result suggests about the burden of the debt.
hints: Use the debt-to-GDP ratio for each year.
Compare the two ratios rather than the two debt figures when judging the burden.
questions.targets: Debt level vs debt relative to GDP

table.caption: Table 7: Government debt and nominal GDP of Veld

marking_points: The ratio is unchanged, so although debt rose, the burden relative to the size of the economy did not increase [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer calculates 30% for both years and notes that the debt burden relative to GDP is unchanged even though the debt itself grew.

questions.prompt: The government of Kuva sells bonds to a pension fund. Which statement is correct?
hints: Identify who issues the bond and who holds it.
Follow the money: who receives funds now, and who receives payments later?
questions.targets: Roles of issuer and holder of a bond

options.text: The government is the lender and the pension fund is the borrower
options.misconception: The roles are reversed: the one who issues the bond receives the money.

options.text: The pension fund pays interest to the government until the bond matures
options.misconception: Interest flows to the bondholder, not from it.

options.text: The government must pay interest to the pension fund and repay the amount borrowed on the maturity date
The government never has to repay the amount borrowed, only the interest
options.misconception: A bond has a maturity date on which the amount borrowed is repaid.

questions.prompt: Define the term sustainable debt.
hints: Think about the payments that come with debt and whether the government can keep making them.
A full definition also mentions what happens to the wider economy while those payments are made.
questions.targets: Precise definition of sustainable debt
marking_points: A level of debt at which the government has enough revenue to meet its debt obligations (interest and repayment) without falling into arrears [1]
While still allowing economic growth to continue at an acceptable rate [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer mentions meeting interest and repayment without arrears and the continuation of acceptable economic growth.

questions.prompt: A credit rating agency downgrades the government of Veld's credit rating. What is the most likely consequence?
hints: A credit rating is an assessment of the borrower's ability to repay.
Think about how lenders respond when they judge a borrower to be riskier.
questions.targets: Link between credit rating and cost of borrowing

options.text: Veld's government can borrow more cheaply than before
options.misconception: A downgrade signals higher risk, which does not make borrowing cheaper.

options.text: Veld's existing debt is cancelled by lenders
options.misconception: A rating is an assessment, not a debt cancellation.

options.text: Veld's budget moves automatically into surplus
options.misconception: A rating change does not change tax revenue or spending directly.

options.text: Veld's government must offer higher interest rates on new bonds

questions.prompt: Which situation is most likely to make Kuva's government debt less sustainable?
hints: Consider what happens to debt servicing costs and to tax revenue.
For each option, compare what happens to the cost of servicing the debt with what happens to the government's ability to pay.
questions.targets: Factors affecting debt sustainability

options.text: Real GDP grows faster than the interest rate paid on the debt
options.misconception: Faster growth raises tax revenue and GDP, so the debt burden tends to fall.

options.text: The government runs a budget surplus for several years
options.misconception: Surpluses reduce the debt.

options.text: Kuva's credit rating is upgraded
options.misconception: An upgrade usually lowers borrowing costs.

options.text: Interest rates on government bonds rise while economic growth slows

questions.prompt: Explain two possible consequences for the economy of Veld if its government debt becomes very high.
hints: Think about debt servicing and how lenders view a heavily indebted government.
For each consequence, name it and then show the chain of effects on the economy or government spending.
questions.targets: Consequences of high government debt
marking_points: Consequence 1, e.g. debt servicing takes a larger share of government revenue [1]
Explained, e.g. there is an opportunity cost as less is left for health care, education or infrastructure, which can slow growth [1]
Consequence 2, e.g. credit rating is downgraded / future taxes must rise [1]
Explained, e.g. borrowing costs rise, making the debt harder to repay, or higher taxes reduce consumption and investment [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives two different consequences, each explained with a clear effect on the government or the wider economy.

questions.prompt: Explain how a downgrade in its credit rating could make Kuva's government debt less sustainable.
hints: Start from what a credit rating tells lenders.
Link the lenders' reaction to the cost of new borrowing, then to debt servicing and the government's budget.
questions.targets: Credit rating to borrowing cost to sustainability chain
marking_points: A downgrade signals a higher risk that the government may not repay [1]
Lenders demand higher interest rates on new government bonds [1]
Debt servicing costs rise, so more revenue goes to interest and it becomes harder to meet obligations without further borrowing [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer links the downgrade to higher interest rates and then to higher debt servicing costs that threaten sustainability.

questions.prompt: Veld's economy is growing rapidly and real GDP is now above its full employment level. Which macroeconomic objective is most likely to conflict with this growth?
hints: Think of an AD/AS diagram where output is beyond the full employment level.
For each objective, ask whether it usually improves or worsens when output keeps rising beyond that level.
questions.targets: Growth vs inflation conflict

options.text: Low and stable inflation
Low unemployment
options.misconception: Rapid growth usually lowers unemployment, so these objectives tend to support each other.

options.text: A reduction in government debt
options.misconception: Growth raises tax revenue, which usually helps reduce the debt burden.

options.text: A rise in real GDP per capita
options.misconception: Rapid growth in real GDP usually raises real GDP per capita.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most likely to be a cost of rapid economic growth in Kuva?
hints: Think about what happens to natural capital when production expands quickly.
Rule out options that describe what usually happens in a slowdown rather than a boom.
questions.targets: Environmental costs of growth

options.text: A fall in tax revenue collected by the government
options.misconception: Growth raises incomes and spending, so tax revenue usually rises.

options.text: A rise in cyclical unemployment
options.misconception: Cyclical unemployment rises in a downturn, not when output grows rapidly.

options.text: A fall in the average price level
options.misconception: Rapid growth tends to put upward, not downward, pressure on prices.

options.text: Faster depletion of forests and non-renewable resources

questions.prompt: Using an AD/AS diagram described in words, explain why rapid economic growth in Veld may conflict with the objective of low inflation.
hints: Use an AD/AS diagram with the economy near or beyond full employment output.
Describe which curve shifts, what happens to real output and the price level, and why the price effect is large.
questions.targets: Growth vs low inflation, demand-pull
marking_points: Rapid growth driven by rising AD is shown as a rightward shift of the AD curve [1]
Real output rises but the price level also rises [1]
As the economy approaches or passes full employment, resources become scarce and costs rise [1]
So further increases in AD mainly raise the price level, causing demand-pull inflation / an inflationary gap [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer describes a rightward AD shift near full employment and explains why the price level rises, linking this to demand-pull inflation.

questions.prompt: Explain why the pursuit of rapid economic growth in Kuva may conflict with environmental sustainability.
hints: Think about what happens to natural capital and ecological resources as output expands.
Link more production to resource use or pollution, then to the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
questions.targets: Growth vs environmental sustainability
marking_points: Higher output requires more use of natural resources, e.g. forests, minerals, fossil fuels [1]
Production and consumption create more pollution / damage to ecological resources such as clean air, soil and biodiversity [1]
Natural capital is depleted, reducing the ability of future generations to meet their needs [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer links growth to resource depletion and pollution, and then to reduced sustainability for future generations.

questions.prompt: Which scenario best shows a conflict between economic growth and an equitable distribution of income in Veld?
hints: Look for growth happening together with a change in how income is shared.
For each option, ask whether income shares change and, if so, in which direction.
questions.targets: Growth vs equity conflict

options.text: Real GDP falls and unemployment rises across all regions
options.misconception: This is a recession, where growth is absent rather than in conflict with equity.

options.text: Real GDP rises and the incomes of all groups rise by the same percentage
options.misconception: If all incomes rise by the same percentage, income shares stay the same.

options.text: Real GDP rises, but most of the extra income goes to the richest 10% of households
Real GDP rises and the government uses extra tax revenue to raise transfer payments
options.misconception: This shows growth supporting a fairer distribution, not conflicting with it.

questions.prompt: The government of Kuva cuts its spending sharply to reduce its budget deficit. Explain why this may conflict with the objectives of economic growth and low unemployment.
hints: Government spending is one of the components of aggregate demand.
Trace the effect of the spending cut through AD to real output and then to the demand for labour.
questions.targets: Deficit reduction vs growth and unemployment
marking_points: Lower government spending reduces aggregate demand, shifting AD to the left [1]
Real output falls or grows more slowly, reducing economic growth [1]
Firms need fewer workers, so (cyclical) unemployment rises [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer links the spending cut to a fall in AD, then to lower real output and higher unemployment.
